account.bio: Evergreen tips for our launch destinations, from the Travel Buddy team.

posts.body: Ride the cable car up Sugarloaf in the late afternoon: you get daylight views over Guanabara Bay and can stay for sunset as the city lights come on. Weekdays are calmer.
On Sundays the main road through Aterro do Flamengo closes to cars and fills with cyclists, runners and families. Rent a bike and ride towards Botafogo with Sugarloaf ahead of you.
Set up a rechargeable IC card or a mobile Suica/PASMO on day one. It works on almost every train, subway and bus in Tokyo and at many shops, so you can skip ticket machines.
Eat like office workers: department-store food halls (depachika) on the basement floors sell bento, sushi and sweets, and many discount prepared food in the evening before closing.
See the famous temples at opening time or in the last hour before closing. Fushimi Inari's gates are open around the clock, so an early-morning walk up the mountain is the quietest way to see them.
Rent a bicycle: Kyoto is flat, compact and laid out on a grid, and riding along the Kamo River between neighbourhoods is often quicker than the bus at busy times.
Lisbon is built on hills and its limestone pavements (calçada) get slippery. Wear shoes with grip, and use the funiculars and Tram 28 to save your legs on the steepest climbs.
Try pastéis de nata warm from the oven with a dusting of cinnamon. Belém is famous for them, but bakeries all over the city make excellent ones.
Book Sagrada Família and Park Güell online in advance: entry is by timed slot and same-day tickets often sell out.
Dinner starts late here. Bridge the gap the local way with a vermut and a few small plates in the early evening, especially at weekends.
Book timed-entry tickets online for the Louvre and other big museums; walk-up queues can be long. Free-entry rules vary by age and residency, so check each museum's site before you buy.
Swap one restaurant lunch for a picnic: bread, cheese and fruit from a market or bakery, eaten by the Seine or along Canal Saint-Martin, where locals gather on warm evenings.
Carry a refillable bottle: Rome's street fountains (nasoni) run with free drinking water. Block the spout with a finger and the water arcs up from the hole on top.
Churches, including St. Peter's Basilica, ask visitors to cover shoulders and knees. A light scarf in your bag solves it on hot days.
On Sunday mornings Paseo de la Reforma closes to cars for cyclists, skaters and walkers. Borrow a bike and ride towards Chapultepec park.
The city sits at about 2,240 m. Take your first day slowly, drink plenty of water and go easy on alcohol while you adjust to the altitude.
Cusco is at roughly 3,400 m. Plan a gentle first day, or start lower in the Sacred Valley and work your way up before any big hikes.
Machu Picchu admits a limited number of visitors per day with timed tickets, so book well ahead, especially for the dry season.
Medina alleys aren't always labelled and maps can lag behind. Use big landmarks such as the Koutoubia minaret and Jemaa el-Fnaa square to get your bearings.
Arrive at Jemaa el-Fnaa around sunset, when the food stalls fire up their grills and musicians and storytellers gather. Watch it from a rooftop café first, then dive in.
Table Mountain's cableway closes in strong wind, which can pick up quickly. Check its status and go up on the first clear morning instead of saving it for your last day.
Drive the coastal road towards Cape Point and stop at Boulders Beach to watch the African penguin colony from the boardwalks.
Use the river: Chao Phraya Express boats link many sights along the water and skip the road traffic. The orange-flag boats are the simplest option for visitors.
The Grand Palace and temples such as Wat Pho require covered shoulders and knees. Pack a light layer for temple days.
Walk the coastal path from Bondi to Coogee: about 6 km of clifftops, beaches and ocean pools. In summer, start early for cooler air.
Take the ferry from Circular Quay to Manly for views of the Opera House and Harbour Bridge at a fraction of the price of a harbour cruise.
The subway runs around the clock. Tap a contactless card or phone at the turnstile (OMNY) instead of buying a separate ticket.
Walk the Brooklyn Bridge from Brooklyn towards Manhattan so the skyline is ahead of you, then wander DUMBO's waterfront park.
Weather changes fast. Pack layers and a waterproof shell even in summer, and check road and weather conditions before driving out of the city.
Do as locals do and spend an evening at a neighbourhood geothermal pool, with hot tubs and outdoor lanes. Showering without a swimsuit before you get in is the rule.
Walk the promenade's famous wave-patterned mosaic at dawn or dusk, and stop at a beach kiosk for fresh coconut water.
Stay for sunset on Arpoador rock at the end of Ipanema beach. When the sun dips behind the mountains, the crowd often breaks into applause.
Santa Teresa's hilly cobbled streets are full of artists' studios and small bars. Ride the restored bondinho tram up from the city centre.
Visit Senso-ji early in the morning or after dark, when the temple is lit up and the crowds along Nakamise shopping street have thinned out.
Watch Shibuya Crossing from above first, then cross it yourself. Evenings are the busiest and most spectacular time.
Lose yourself in Alfama's stairways and alleys, then end the evening with fado in one of the neighbourhood's small restaurants.

Follow the line of cobblestones that marks where the Wall stood, then visit the Berlin Wall Memorial on Bernauer Strasse: the preserved strip and watchtower explain the division better than any museum.
Rent a bike and ride across Tempelhofer Feld, the old airport turned park. The runways are open to everyone, and on windy days kite surfers race along them.
Most of London's big museums are free, including the British Museum, the National Gallery and the Natural History Museum. Go right at opening time for the popular rooms.
Walk the South Bank from Westminster Bridge to Tower Bridge: street performers, the Tate Modern, Shakespeare's Globe and Borough Market are all on the way.
Many milongas, the tango dance halls, start with a beginners' class early in the evening. Stay afterwards to watch the locals dance until late.
Recoleta Cemetery is a maze of grand mausoleums; take a map at the entrance and pair it with a walk through the nearby parks and cafes of Recoleta.
